# Azure KeyVault Administration client module for Go

>**Note:** The Administration module only works with [Managed HSM][managed_hsm] – functions targeting a Key Vault will fail.

* Managed HSM administration (this module) - role-based access control (RBAC), settings, vault-level backup and restore options, and External Key Manager (EKM) connection management
* Certificate management ([azcertificates](https://aka.ms/azsdk/go/keyvault-certificates/docs)) - create, manage, and deploy public and private SSL/TLS certificates
* Cryptographic key management ([azkeys](https://aka.ms/azsdk/go/keyvault-keys/docs)) - create, store, and control access to the keys used to encrypt your data
* Secrets management ([azsecrets](https://aka.ms/azsdk/go/keyvault-secrets/docs)) - securely store and control access to tokens, passwords, certificates, API keys, and other secrets

Azure Key Vault Managed HSM is a fully-managed, highly-available, single-tenant, standards-compliant cloud service that enables you to safeguard
cryptographic keys for your cloud applications using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs.

The Azure Key Vault administration library clients support administrative tasks such as full backup / restore, key-level role-based access control (RBAC), settings management, and External Key Manager (EKM) connection management.

[Source code][azadmin_repo] | [Package (pkg.go.dev)][azadmin_pkg_go]| [Product documentation][managed_hsm_docs] | Samples ([backup][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_backup], [rbac][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_rbac], [settings][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_settings], ekm - TBD)

## Getting started

### Install the package

Install `azadmin` and `azidentity` with `go get`:
```
go get github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/security/keyvault/azadmin
go get github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/azidentity
```
[azidentity][azure_identity] is used for Azure Active Directory authentication. It creates a credential which is passed to the client contructor as shown in the examples below.


### Prerequisites

* An [Azure subscription][azure_sub].
* A supported Go version (the Azure SDK supports the two most recent Go releases)
* An existing [Key Vault Managed HSM][managed_hsm]. If you need to create one, you can do so [using the Azure CLI][create_managed_hsm].

### Authentication

This document demonstrates using [azidentity.NewDefaultAzureCredential][default_cred_ref] to authenticate. This credential type works in both local development and production environments. We recommend using a [managed identity][managed_identity] in production.

The clients accept any [azidentity][azure_identity] credential. See the [azidentity][azure_identity] documentation for more information about other credential types.

#### Create a client

Constructing the client also requires your Managed HSM's URL, which you can get from the Azure CLI or the Azure Portal.

- [Example backup client](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/security/keyvault/azadmin/backup#example-NewClient)
- [Example rbac client][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_rbac]
- [Example settings client](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/security/keyvault/azadmin/settings#example-NewClient)
- Example ekm client - TBD

## Key concepts

### RoleDefinition

A `RoleDefinition` is a collection of permissions. A role definition defines the operations that can be performed, such as read, write, and delete. It can also define the operations that are excluded from allowed operations.

A `RoleDefinition` can be listed and specified as part of a `RoleAssignment`.

### RoleAssignment

A `RoleAssignment` is the association of a RoleDefinition to a service principal. They can be created, listed, fetched individually, and deleted.

### rbac.Client

An `rbac.Client` manages `RoleDefinition` and `RoleAssignment` types.

### backup.Client

A `backup.Client` performs full key backups, full key restores, and selective key restores.

### settings.Client

A `settings.Client` provides methods to update, get, and list settings for a Managed HSM.

### ekm.KeyVaultClient

An `ekm.KeyVaultClient` manages the External Key Manager (EKM) connection on a Managed HSM. Use it to configure the proxy through which the HSM accesses externally-managed keys, to retrieve the client certificate the HSM presents to the proxy, and to verify connectivity to the proxy.

## Examples

Get started with our examples:
- [backup][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_backup]  
- [rbac][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_rbac]
- [settings][azadmin_pkg_go_samples_settings]
- ekm - TBD

## Troubleshooting

### Error Handling

All methods which send HTTP requests return `*azcore.ResponseError` when these requests fail. `ResponseError` has error details and the raw response from Key Vault.

```go
import "github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/azcore"

settings, err := client.GetSettings(context.Background(), nil)
if err != nil {
    var httpErr *azcore.ResponseError
    if errors.As(err, &httpErr) {
        // TODO: investigate httpErr
    } else {
        // TODO: not an HTTP error
    }
}
```

### Logging

This module uses the logging implementation in `azcore`. To turn on logging for all Azure SDK modules, set `AZURE_SDK_GO_LOGGING` to `all`. By default the logger writes to stderr. Use the `azcore/log` package to control log output. For example, logging only HTTP request and response events, and printing them to stdout:

```go
import azlog "github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/azcore/log"

// Print log events to stdout
azlog.SetListener(func(cls azlog.Event, msg string) {
	fmt.Println(msg)
})

// Includes only requests and responses in logs
azlog.SetEvents(azlog.EventRequest, azlog.EventResponse)
```

### Accessing `http.Response`

You can access the raw `*http.Response` returned by Key Vault using the `runtime.WithCaptureResponse` method and a context passed to any client method.

```go
import "github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/azcore/runtime"

var response *http.Response
ctx := runtime.WithCaptureResponse(context.TODO(), &response)
_, err = client.GetSettings(context.Background(), nil)
if err != nil {
    // TODO: handle error
}
// TODO: do something with response
```

proposals.subtype: Build the backup client with a configurable Key Vault challenge policy
proposals.explanation: backup.NewClient defaults nil options, forwards DisableChallengeResourceVerification to NewKeyVaultChallengePolicy and installs that policy PerRetry in azcore.NewClient. It configures the api-version query parameter and Microsoft.KeyVault tracing namespace, then retains vaultURL and the azcore client. This wires an imported policy rather than implementing its challenge algorithm.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: custom_client.go explicitly identifies handwritten additions and provides the complete constructor and option declaration without a generated header.

proposals.subtype: Build the EKM client with configurable challenge resource verification
proposals.explanation: ekm.NewClient defaults options and builds the shared challenge policy with the exposed verification-disable flag. It registers that policy PerRetry, sets api-version query placement and Microsoft.KeyVault tracing, propagates azcore client creation errors and constructs KeyVaultClient with vaultURL. Shared authentication internals are absent.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The custom file explicitly labels itself handwritten and contains executable constructor wiring outside generated files.

proposals.subtype: Build the RBAC client with the shared challenge policy and option forwarding
proposals.explanation: rbac.NewClient accepts the verification-disable option, builds a Key Vault challenge policy, adds it PerRetry and initializes the azcore client with api-version query handling and Microsoft.KeyVault tracing. It returns a client retaining vaultURL. The constructor has no visible vault-URL validation despite the caller-directed documentation.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The supplied complete custom_client.go explicitly declares handwritten additions and shows the concrete constructor.

proposals.explanation: settings.NewClient defaults nil options and passes DisableChallengeResourceVerification to the imported challenge-policy constructor. The policy becomes a PerRetry pipeline policy; API-version query handling, module metadata and tracing namespace are configured before constructing the client. The policy's actual challenge validation/token behavior is not supplied.

proposals.subtype: Use the custom restore handler for new and resumed pre-full restore operations
proposals.explanation: beginPreFullRestore initiates preFullRestore when no resume token is supplied, obtains the shared custom handler and constructs runtime.NewPoller with AzureAsyncOp final-state routing, handler and tracer. Otherwise it creates an empty-response handler and calls NewPollerFromResumeToken with handler and tracer. getHandler returns nil for a Fake-Poller-Status response, otherwise NewRestorePoller.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The custom file explicitly says handwritten additions and the method supplies concrete custom handler wiring rather than only a generated Begin return type.

proposals.subtype: Wire the restore poller into full restore initiation and resumption
proposals.explanation: beginFullRestore invokes fullRestore for a new operation, requests getHandler with AzureAsyncOp and creates NewPoller with the resulting handler and tracer. Unlike the pre-full method, its NewPollerOptions does not explicitly set FinalStateVia. Resume-token calls use getHandler with a nil response and NewPollerFromResumeToken; no resumption implementation is captured.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The handwritten file supplies the method body and explicit custom poller selection, beyond ordinary generated LRO declarations.

proposals.subtype: Wire the restore handler into selective-key restore and resume paths
proposals.explanation: beginSelectiveKeyRestore forwards keyName and restore parameters to selectiveKeyRestore for a new operation, obtains the custom handler and returns NewPoller with handler/tracer. On resume it obtains an empty-response handler and calls NewPollerFromResumeToken. As with full restore, NewPollerOptions itself does not explicitly set FinalStateVia.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The explicitly handwritten method implements both branches and attaches the custom handler.

proposals.subtype: Initialize custom restore polling state from the initial response
proposals.explanation: NewRestorePoller accepts nil response to produce a pipeline-only handler for rehydration. Otherwise it requires Azure-AsyncOperation, calls IsValidURL, obtains provisioning state while discarding that helper's error and falls back to StatusInProgress if empty. It retains response, async/location/original URLs, request method, final-state option and current state. Resume-token decoding and helper internals are not supplied.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: restore_poller.go explicitly identifies handwritten additions and a custom restore poller; the full constructor is captured.

proposals.subtype: Poll the async URL and retain explicit operation status
proposals.explanation: restorePoller.Poll uses pollHelper to issue GET to AsyncURL. Invalid status codes update p.resp and return NewResponseError; missing status is an error, and a valid nonempty status updates both response and CurState. Done delegates terminal-state classification to the shared helper. Status/URL classifiers are imported and their semantics are not inferred.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The explicitly handwritten restore-poller file implements the status transition and polling callback, not simply a generated poller reference.

proposals.subtype: Decode the last polling response without an additional final-resource request
proposals.explanation: restorePoller.Result returns nil immediately for 204, then returns NewResponseError for failed state, otherwise delegates the last response to resultHelper. That helper again short-circuits 204, arranges body close, errors on invalid status/failed state, accepts empty payloads and JSON-decodes nonempty payloads into out. Neither body performs a final GET using LocURL/OrigURL/FinalState. The supplied result types are absent.
proposals.handwrittenRationale: The handwritten restore-poller file supplies both the result method and its decoding helper, demonstrating concrete custom result handling.

decisions.reason: The handwritten backup constructor and option declaration at lines 22-58 pass the verification flag into the imported challenge policy and install it PerRetry. This supports client-side challenge-policy wiring, not a claim that this file implements the policy itself.
The EKM constructor at lines 16-52 separately exposes the challenge-verification option and installs a shared challenge policy in its pipeline; the file identifies these additions as handwritten.

The handwritten RBAC constructor at lines 16-52 forwards the verification option to the imported challenge policy and attaches it PerRetry. The proposal does not claim that the documented caller-side vault URL check happens in the constructor.

The settings constructor at lines 14-52 is explicitly identified as handwritten, forwards the verification flag, and installs the imported challenge policy. Actual challenge validation remains outside the captured code.
The handwritten ErrorInfo declaration and UnmarshalJSON implementation at lines 60-79 visibly retain the incoming bytes and decode Code into the custom error type; no defensive copy is shown.
The separate handwritten Error method at lines 81-85 returns the entire retained JSON as its error string. This is observable error presentation distinct from the preceding JSON-decoding method.

The handwritten pre-full restore method at lines 99-127 supplies a custom handler to both new and resumed pollers, with the fake-response exception in getHandler at lines 87-97. It is not merely a generated LRO declaration.

Lines 129-156 implement new and resume-token full-restore branches around getHandler. The source confirms that the new-poller options do not explicitly include FinalStateVia; behavior inside runtime.NewPoller is not asserted.

The handwritten selective-key restore method at lines 158-185 passes the key name to the underlying operation and attaches the custom handler on new and resumed pollers. This is a separate operation instance of the reusable custom-poller pattern.

The handwritten NewRestorePoller at lines 66-122 validates an Azure-AsyncOperation URL, sets a default in-progress state, and records polling context; for nil response it constructs a pipeline-only handler. No unseen resume-token decoding is claimed.

The handwritten pollHelper, Done and Poll implementations at the cited lines GET the async URL, reject invalid or missing status, update response and state, and defer terminal-state classification to an imported helper.

The handwritten Result and resultHelper at the cited lines handle empty 204 responses, failed states and JSON payloads from the retained response. Neither captured method makes a separate final-resource request.

limitations: Coverage is partial: eight of 45 eligible files from 82 discovered files are captured across backup, EKM, RBAC and settings. No complete-library absence conclusion is possible.
Evidence kinds are unknown, but custom-client/poller files explicitly label themselves handwritten, match the supplied Go convention and contain concrete implementations without generated headers.

The four constructors wire an imported Key Vault challenge policy; its implementation, challenge-domain enforcement and token acquisition are not captured. Caller-directed vault URL validation comments do not establish validation in these constructors. Options, API-version placement and tracing are grouped with constructor wiring rather than double counted.

Three fake/custom_server.go files set serverTransportInterceptor to an imported FakeChallenge in init. They demonstrate fake-server setup, not a production authentication-policy implementation. The interceptor's body and callers are absent, so they are not proposed as additional production customizations.

getHandler's Fake-Poller-Status bypass is included as context for the real restore entrypoints, not as a separate production customization or proof of runtime fake handling. Public callers of the lowercase begin methods and generated operations are not captured.

The three Begin implementations and the custom handler's initialization, status progression and final-response decoding are distinct supplied source units. Shared helpers are cited with their consuming unit rather than counted again as generic transport/JSON utilities.

Runtime NewPoller, resume-token serialization/rehydration, status classification, URL validation, provisioning-state/status parsing and response-error creation are imported. No accepted protocol, status vocabulary, resume format or end-to-end safety claim is inferred.

The custom Result uses the retained response and gives 204 success precedence over failed-state handling; it does not visibly use stored LocURL/OrigURL/Method/FinalState for a final request. This is literal source behavior, not a root-cause diagnosis or implementation fix.
ErrorInfo retains the raw input slice even before JSON parsing succeeds. Operation integration and ownership/lifetime of that slice are not supplied.

No SDK or tool was executed and no external source was fetched. Addressability reflects plausible generation hooks for policy wiring, custom LRO handlers and error representation, not measured support or reducibility.
